paragraphs.source_en: “It has been a long time since I last came to call on you. The truth is, I have been terribly busy since the end of last year; I kept meaning to come, but somehow my feet never turned in this direction.” The newly arrived visitor toyed with the cord of his formal haori and said something quite enigmatic. My master asked with a grave face, “And in what direction do your feet turn?” As he spoke, he tugged at the cuff of his black cotton formal haori. This cotton haori of his was short in the sleeves, and from below it a coarse silk kimono protruded about half an inch on either side. “Heh, heh, heh, it is in rather a different direction.” Kangetsu said with a laugh. Looking at him, I saw that today one of the gentleman’s front teeth was missing. So my master changed the subject and asked, “I say! What happened to your tooth?” “Well, I was eating shiitake mushrooms somewhere.” “Eating what, did you say?” “Well, I ate a little shiitake. When I tried to bite through the cap with my front teeth, snap, the tooth broke.” My master said, “A tooth breaking off from biting a shiitake? That makes you sound positively old. It might make a haiku, but it will never do for love.” As he said this, my master lightly tapped my head with his palm. “Ah, so this is that cat? He has grown quite fat! Even compared with the rickshaw man’s big black cat, he does not seem at all inferior. A fine creature indeed.” Mr. Kangetsu praised me lavishly. “He has grown a good deal lately,” my master said, proudly thumping me on the head. I was naturally pleased to be praised, but my head hurt rather badly. Kangetsu returned to his former topic and said, “The night before last we held another little ensemble concert.” My master asked, “Where?” “You had better not ask the address. Three violins, with piano accompaniment. It was quite enjoyable. With three violins, even if they are played rather badly, they can still be listened to. Two of the players were women, and I was mixed in among them; even I thought I played with considerable spirit.” My master asked, as though envious, “Oh, and who were those two women?” Although my master usually wears a face like a withered tree or a cold cliff, in truth he is by no means indifferent to women. He once read a Western novel in which a certain character appeared who fell at least a little in love with nearly every woman. The novel said satirically, “When one reckoned it up, he had felt amorous toward nearly seven-tenths of the women who passed along the street.” My master greatly admired this, saying, “That is the truth.” Why a man so full of worldly desires should live like an oyster is more than a cat like me can understand. Some say it is because he once had his heart broken; others say it is because of his weak stomach; still others say it is because he has neither money nor courage. Whichever guess is right, he is not a person important enough to concern the history of Meiji, so it hardly matters. Still, it is a fact that he inquired, in an envious tone, about the women with whom Kangetsu had been keeping company.

paragraphs.source_zh: “很久没有来看望您啦。我从去年年底一直忙得不可开交，总想来看您，可总没机会到这一带来。”新来的客人摆弄着他那礼装大褂上的丝绦，说些叫人摸不着头脑的话。主人一本正经地问道：“你都去哪一带啦？”边说边扯了扯他那用黑棉布缝制的礼装大褂的袖口，主人的这件棉布礼装大褂，身长很短，下摆处向左右各露出里边半寸长的粗绸袍子。“嘿、嘿、嘿，那方向可有点不同。”寒月笑道。我一看，这位先生今天掉了一颗门牙。于是主人转换话题问道：“喂！你牙齿怎么啦？”“嗯，我在一个地方吃香菇来着。”“你说吃了什么？”“唔，吃了点香菇，我用门牙一咬香菇的盖儿，‘嘣’的一下门牙折断了。”主人说：“咬一下香菇，就崩断了牙？简直成了老头啦。这也许上得了俳句，不过搞恋爱可就不成啦。”主人说着，用手心轻轻拍了一下我的脑袋。“呵，这就是那只猫呀？长得满肥的！和车夫家的大黑猫比一比，也不见得逊色，蛮不错嘛。”寒月君大大夸奖了我一番。“最近又长大了许多，”主人说着，得意地敲着我的脑袋。我受到夸奖，当然很高兴，可是脑袋被敲得挺痛。寒月君又把话题扯回来说道：“前天夜里又搞了一个合奏会。”主人问道：“在哪儿？”“地址您还是别打听为好。三把小提琴，加上钢琴伴奏，蛮有意思。只要有三把小提琴，就是拉得蹩脚些，也能听得过去啊。拉琴的，两个是女的，我夹杂在中间，连我自己也觉得拉得蛮带劲儿哩。”主人羡慕似地问道：“噢，那两个女的是什么人呀？”别看主人平时脸上装出一副枯木寒岩的样子，其实，他可不是个对女性能忘情的人。他曾经读过一本西洋小说，小说中有一个人物，对所有的女人几乎都一见钟情。小说讽刺地写道：“算起来，从街上走过的女人，将近十分之七他都产生过爱慕之情。”主人对这一点大加赞赏，说什么：“这是真理。”如此凡心极重的人，为什么却过着牡蛎一般的生活，这就不是我这个猫所能了解的啦。有人说这是因为他失恋过，又有人说这是因为他患有胃病，还有人说是因为他既无钱又胆怯的缘故。不管是哪种揣测，横竖他不是与明治历史有关的大人物，所以都无关紧要。不过，他带着羡慕的口吻打听寒月君所接触的女性，这毕竟是事实。

paragraphs.source_en: Mr. Kangetsu, with evident pleasure, picked up a slice of fish cake from the relish with his chopsticks and bit off half of it with his front teeth. I was truly worried that he might break another tooth, but this time all was well. Then he replied coolly, “There is no need for you to concern yourself. Both ladies are daughters of distinguished families, and not anyone you know.” “O-o-oh,” my master drew out the sound, omitting the rest, “so that is how it is,” while thinking something over. Kangetsu, perhaps thinking it was time to wind things up, suggested, “It really is fine weather today. If you are free, shall we go out for a walk together? Port Arthur has fallen, and the town is in a great bustle.” My master’s expression seemed to say, “The fall of Port Arthur is of no concern to me; what matters is learning the identities of those two women.” After pondering for a while, he finally made up his mind and said, “Very well, let us go.” With that he rose, still wearing the same cotton formal haori and the padded Yuki silk robe he had worn for twenty years. I hear that padded robe had been left to him as a keepsake when his elder brother died. Sturdy as Yuki silk may be, no cloth can endure such long wear; many places had grown thin, and when held up to the sun one could see the stitches of the patches applied from inside. In my master’s clothing there is no distinction between the twelfth month and New Year, nor between everyday wear and clothes for going out. When he says he is going out, he simply folds his hands in his sleeves and strolls off at ease. Whether this is because he has no other clothes to change into, or because he has them but finds changing too troublesome, I do not know; at least I do not think it is due to a broken heart.
